questions.q: Of whom was the Teacher a descendant?
questions.a: The Teacher was a descendant of David, king in Jerusalem.

questions.q: What does the Teacher say everything is?
questions.a: The Teacher says everything is temporary, fleeting, and insubstantial; the whole of it is vapor.

questions.q: What does the Teacher ask about the benefit of people’s hard work?
questions.a: He asks what profit people gain from all their hard work.

questions.q: What does the sun do every day?
questions.a: The sun rises and sets, and then hurries back to the place where it will rise again.
The wind blows toward the south, then turns toward the north; it goes around and around and returns to where it began.

questions.q: Where do all the rivers go?
questions.a: All the rivers go to the sea, yet the sea never becomes full, and the water keeps flowing.

questions.q: By what is the eye not satisfied?
questions.a: The eye is not satisfied by what it sees or hears.
Whatever has been done in the past is what will be done in the future.

questions.q: What does the Teacher say about something that seems new?
questions.a: The Teacher says that whatever seems new already existed long ago, in times before us.

questions.q: What does the Teacher say about people remembering past generations?
questions.a: The Teacher says no one remembers the people or events of long ago, and future generations will not be remembered by those who come after them either.
The Teacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.

questions.q: To what did the Teacher apply his mind?
questions.a: The Teacher applied his mind to study and to search out by wisdom everything that is done in the world.

questions.q: To what do all the deeds that are done under the sun amount?
questions.a: All the deeds that are done under the sun amount to vapor and an attempt to catch the wind.

questions.q: What does the Teacher say about things that are bent or lacking?
questions.a: He says that what is bent cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

questions.q: What did the Teacher say about his wisdom compared to those who ruled in Jerusalem before him?
questions.a: He said that he had grown and increased in wisdom more than anyone who ruled in Jerusalem before him.

questions.q: What did the Teacher resolve to learn about?
questions.a: He resolved to learn about wisdom, and also about madness and folly.

questions.q: What increases along with a person’s wisdom and knowledge?
questions.a: A person who has much wisdom also has much anger, and one who increases knowledge increases pain.

commentary.text: Solomon shows that all human things are vain. (Eccl. 1:1-3) Man's toil and want of satisfaction. (Eccl. 1:4-8) There is nothing new. (Eccl. 1:9-11) The vexation in pursuit of knowledge. (Eccl. 1:12-18)

Eccl. 1:1-3 Much is to be learned by comparing one part of Scripture with another. We here behold Solomon returning from the broken and empty cisterns of the world, to the Fountain of living water; recording his own folly and shame, the bitterness of his disappointment, and the lessons he had learned. Those that have taken warning to turn and live, should warn others not to go on and die. He does not merely say all things are vain, but that they are vanity. VANITY OF VANITIES, ALL IS VANITY. This is the text of the preacher's sermon, of which in this book he never loses sight. If this world, in its present state, were all, it would not be worth living for; and the wealth and pleasure of this world, if we had ever so much, are not enough to make us happy. What profit has a man of all his labour? All he gets by it will not supply the wants of the soul, nor satisfy its desires; will not atone for the sins of the soul, nor hinder the loss of it: what profit will the wealth of the world be to the soul in death, in judgment, or in the everlasting state?

Eccl. 1:4-8 All things change, and never rest. Man, after all his labour, is no nearer finding rest than the sun, the wind, or the current of the river. His soul will find no rest, if he has it not from God. The senses are soon tired, yet still craving what is untried.

Eccl. 1:9-11 Men's hearts and their corruptions are the same now as in former times; their desires, and pursuits, and complaints, still the same. This should take us from expecting happiness in the creature, and quicken us to seek eternal blessings. How many things and persons in Solomon's day were thought very great, yet there is no remembrance of them now!

Eccl. 1:12-18 Solomon tried all things, and found them vanity. He found his searches after knowledge weariness, not only to the flesh, but to the mind. The more he saw of the works done under the sun, the more he saw their vanity; and the sight often vexed his spirit. He could neither gain that satisfaction to himself, nor do that good to others, which he expected. Even the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom discovered man's wickedness and misery; so that the more he knew, the more he saw cause to lament and mourn. Let us learn to hate and fear sin, the cause of all this vanity and misery; to value Christ; to seek rest in the knowledge, love, and service of the Saviour.
